title: Duplicate product descriptions and SEO: what Google does with manufacturer copy
summary: What Google does when stores share manufacturer descriptions, how to sell on marketplaces and your own site, and which SKUs need unique copy.
body_markdown:
Using the manufacturer's product description won't get your store penalized. Google has said there's no penalty for duplicate content on product pages.


But duplicate copy still has a cost. When several pages carry the same description, Google tends to show only one of them for searches that match that text, and the others get left out. Your page has to win on everything else: price, stock, extra detail and reviews.


So the question is where unique copy is worth the effort, and how to add it without rewriting your whole catalog.


## Is there a duplicate content penalty for product descriptions?


No. Asked about stores that use the manufacturer's description, Google's John Mueller said in a 2021 office hours session that Google "would not penalize a website for having duplicate descriptions" ([Search Engine Journal](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-duplicate-product-descriptions/420899/) ). He added that penalties are for sites made up entirely of copied content, and that a store using the same description as the manufacturer is fine as long as the rest of its site is its own.


[Google's own documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) says the same thing: some duplicate content on a site is normal and doesn't break its spam policies.


The exception is a site built almost entirely from copied content. Google's[spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) list scraping, meaning republishing other sites' content without adding anything, and thin affiliate pages that copy product descriptions straight from the merchant. A store with its own pages and stock that uses some manufacturer copy isn't in that group.


## What does Google do when several stores use the same description?


Google groups pages whose main content is the same or very similar, then picks one to show. Its documentation says it chooses the page it judges most complete and useful for the searcher.


Take a cordless drill sold by 50 retailers, all using the brand's description. If someone searches for a phrase that appears only in that description, Google is likely to show one or two of those pages, not all 50. Mueller said the choice can come down to things like which store has the product in stock, or which is the local option for the searcher.


Searches that don't match the shared text work differently. A page that adds the drill's battery runtime and which batteries it works with can show up for searches the other 49 pages can't answer.


## Can you use the same description on Amazon and on your own site?


Yes. There's no penalty for it. The catch is that your product page and your Amazon listing then compete for the same searches, and Google may choose to show the marketplace listing.


If your own site matters more to you, give it the fuller version. Keep the core facts the same everywhere, and add the detail you have that the marketplace listing doesn't, such as how it compares with your other models, or answers to the questions customers ask.


## Should brands write different copy for their own site and for retailers?


Most brands supply product copy to their retailers, so the same description ends up on many retailer pages. That's normal, and retailers often prefer it because it saves them work.


A brand's own site has room to go further than the version it hands out. It can include the full spec sheet, plus guidance only the brand can give, such as care instructions or how the product compares across the range. That gives the brand's page a reason to rank for searches the retailer pages don't cover.


Many brands keep one approved core description and adapt it for each channel's length and format rules. Retailers that accept extra brand content, such as Amazon A+ Content, give you space for more on their pages too. Our guide to[enhanced content](https://www.hypotenuse.ai/blog/enhanced-content-ecommerce) covers how that works.


## Do you need unique copy for every SKU?


Not always. For a large catalog, it makes sense to start where unique copy is most likely to pay off:


- Products that already get search traffic or drive a lot of revenue
- Products sold by many other stores, where you need a reason to be the page that shows up
- Products you know better than others, so you have something real to add
- New products, where nobody has published much yet


For long-tail products, the manufacturer's description plus complete, accurate attributes may be enough. Filters and site search run on attributes, so those still need to be right.


Variants are a separate case. A drill sold in two battery sizes doesn't need two rewritten descriptions. One description for the product, with the differences held as attributes, usually works better. Our guide to[product variant descriptions](https://www.hypotenuse.ai/blog/product-variant-descriptions) goes into detail.


## How do you make a product description unique without rewriting everything?


Add information other pages don't have. Things you can add include:


- **Details others leave out.** What's in the box, or which batteries and accessories it works with.
- **Use cases for your customers.** Which jobs the drill suits, and which it doesn't.
- **Answers to common questions.** Pull them from support tickets and reviews.
- **Notes from returns.** If customers return a product because it runs small or doesn't fit a certain model, say so on the page.


Swapping words in copied text doesn't help. Google's spam policies name lightly reworded copied content as a form of scraping, and it gives shoppers nothing new.


## How do duplicate descriptions affect AI search?


AI assistants and AI search features answer shopping questions by drawing on many pages. If your page says the same thing as dozens of others, it gives them no particular reason to cite yours.


Specific details help. Facts like battery runtime and compatibility, or answers to real customer questions, are what AI answers can quote. Structured, complete attributes also help AI shopping tools match your products to what people ask for.


## What about duplicate descriptions within your own site?


Duplicates inside one site usually come from the same product appearing at several URLs, for example through filter and tracking parameters, or one product listed in several categories.


Pick one URL for each product and point the others to it with a[canonical tag](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) , and link to that URL from your own pages. Google may still choose a different page if the signals point elsewhere, but a consistent setup makes its choice easier.

## FAQs


### Is it okay to copy manufacturer product descriptions?


Yes. Google doesn't penalize stores for it. But it does mean your page competes with every other page using the same text, so add your own details to the products that matter most.


### How much duplicate content is acceptable?


Google doesn't set a percentage. A store with its own pages and stock that uses some manufacturer copy is fine. A site built almost entirely from copied content is what Google's spam policies target.


### Do duplicate product descriptions hurt rankings?


Not as a penalty. The effect is that Google usually shows only one of several identical pages for searches that match the shared text, so other parts of your page have to make it the one that shows.
